candidateRows: The freedom relevant to moral responsibility is compatible with determinism and consists in ordinary responsible agency rather than libertarian metaphysics.
This establishes the compatibilist answer to the motion by separating responsibility-grounding freedom from indeterministic or agent-causal freedom.
Harris's earlier portrayal of Dennett's compatibilism as quasi-theological and as failing to acknowledge that free will is unreal.
Dennett stresses extensive agreement about rejecting libertarianism, then locates valuable freedom in competent, uncoerced agency that supports contracts, responsibility, and justified punishment.
Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic meaning of free will by refining inherited concepts instead of treating their magical interpretations as definitive.
This supplies the conceptual methodology behind Dennett's position and explains why rejecting a magical definition need not require abandoning free-will language.
Harris's claim that compatibilism resembles theology and does not identify a serious form of free will.
Dennett treats disputes over whether consciousness or free will exists as partly diplomatic choices between eliminating a misleading concept and retaining a purified naturalistic version.
Compatibilism risks changing the subject because purifying a concept can discard features that are indispensable to what people mean by free will.
This frames Harris's principal conceptual objection: the compatibilist phenomenon may be real while failing to answer the original free-will concern.
Dennett's claim that free will can truthfully be said to exist once its magical and traditional baggage is removed.
Harris distinguishes scientifically explaining a real phenomenon from redefining it so extensively that the supposedly preserved concept no longer addresses its core concern.
Free will is the reasons-responsive competence to control an agent's many practical degrees of freedom, and this capacity—not indeterminism—grounds responsibility.
This is the central positive compatibilist model, connecting freedom, rational control, self-control, absence of usurpation, and moral responsibility.
Harris's objection that compatibilism merely changes the subject by eliminating the concept's essential incompatibilist feature.

Dennett rejects a sharp line between clarification and subject change, then models freedom through controllable capacities, responsiveness to reasons, and the distinction between competent agents and constrained or controlled ones.
The enduring free-will problem concerns first-person authorship and the ability to do otherwise, neither of which is supported by determinism or indeterminism.
This identifies the experiential and metaphysical target Harris believes compatibilism misses and gives his direct argument against conscious authorship.
Dennett's account of free will as reasons-responsive control that can be fully distinguished within either a deterministic or indeterministic world.

Harris separates first-person experience from third-person functional description, denies that an exact replay permits another choice, and argues that thoughts simply arise from unconscious processes.
Compatibilism preserves real capacities but calls them free will in the way one might preserve Sicily while abandoning the fictional features that made Atlantis the subject of interest.
The analogy sharpens the subject-changing objection by conceding compatibilist facts while denying that they answer the motivating first-person claim.
Dennett's proposal to retain free-will language for naturalistic capacities after removing libertarian and magical commitments.
Harris compares rejecting libertarian freedom while retaining compatibilist agency to rejecting mythical Atlantis while redirecting attention to a real island sharing peripheral features.

A nonmagical form of free will preserves the responsibility distinctions people need, while the experience of deciding requires treating some possibilities as open without requiring absolute metaphysical openness.
This directly answers both the subject-changing charge and the experiential challenge by arguing that practical agency supplies the freedom worth preserving.
Harris's Atlantis analogy and his claim that people's felt ability to do otherwise is the indispensable feature compatibilism abandons.
Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that naturalistic agency retains daily responsibility practices and that deliberation necessarily represents alternatives as unsettled.
An agent can meaningfully have been able to do otherwise when a small variation would produce another choice, even if the decision process itself is deterministic.
This provides a concrete compatibilist analysis of alternative possibilities and separates unlucky outcomes from defects in an agent's decision-making design.
Harris's exact-replay standard under which an agent could not have done otherwise unless the identical prior state produced a different result.

A deterministic chess program can lose after one pseudo-random result while remaining well designed; nearby variations support an ordinary counterfactual sense in which it could have chosen differently.
Dependence of major life choices on minute neural differences is deeply subversive of ordinary personhood because it makes the universe, rather than a conscious self, control the outcome.
This explains why accepting compatibilist counterfactuals does not resolve Harris's concern: causal sensitivity itself revives the loss-of-authorship problem.
Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that tiny variations can justify saying a well-designed agent could have acted otherwise.

Harris accepts the functional analysis but argues that tiny neurophysiological contingencies controlling transformative choices conflict with how people experience themselves as authors of their lives.
Neither absolute indeterminacy nor sensitivity to tiny changes defeats freedom: close decisions may flip under small variations, while reason-dominated decisions require much larger changes.
This distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions settled by reasons and argues that determination can express, rather than negate, responsible agency.
Harris's claim that minute physical contingencies behind consequential choices restore marionette-like control by the universe and undermine personhood.

Dennett calls absolute undetermination irrelevant, distinguishes finely balanced choices from strongly reason-governed ones, and begins using a determined yet responsibility-affirming decision as a counterexample.
Chance can settle genuinely balanced decisions without undermining responsibility, while strongly reason-supported decisions remain robust against small physical variations.
This establishes the compatibilist distinction between unavoidable local luck and the reasons-responsive control sufficient for freedom and responsibility.
Harris's claim that microscopic causal differences can redirect important choices and expose the absence of authorship.
Dennett treats borderline choices as possible toss-ups, rejects libertarian indeterminacy, and argues that accepting responsibility never requires complete control over every element of deliberation.
Although undetermined choices would not be free, tiny unchosen neural differences can still determine consequential actions and radically alter a life.
The move accepts the critique of libertarianism while challenging the claim that consequential causal divergence occurs only in harmlessly balanced decisions.
Dennett's position that microscopic variation matters chiefly in genuine toss-ups and does not threaten responsible agency.
Harris agrees that randomness cannot supply authorship but argues that small differences in sleep or neural state can decide whether someone performs a life-changing act.
Complete causal understanding would make ordinary wrongdoing resemble the exculpatory brain-tumor case because no agent authors the decisive neural conditions.
This directly advances the core no-libertarian-free-will case by extending causal non-authorship from exceptional pathology to every human action.
Dennett's claim that practical responsibility survives luck because agents can exercise differing degrees of self-control.
Harris distinguishes their rival responses to incoherent libertarian freedom, then argues from Charles Whitman's tumor to the exculpatory force of complete neurophysiological explanation.
Being causally wired is not equivalent to being impaired, so exceptional neurological disability cannot justify treating every normally capable agent as exculpated.
The response protects compatibilist responsibility by denying that universal causation erases the functional capacity distinction on which accountability rests.
Harris's argument that complete neurophysiology makes all conduct exculpatory in the same sense as Charles Whitman's tumor.
Dennett says neuroscience shows that people are wired, not universally wired wrongly, and maintains a revisable but durable boundary between adequate agency and disabling impairment.
Differences in capacity remain real, but genes, upbringing, environment, and each persuasive input are unchosen, making ultimate blame unjustified while pragmatic accountability remains useful.
This supplies Harris's main reconciliation of causal non-authorship with contracts, restraint, and behavior-shaping sanctions rather than ultimate desert.
Dennett's assertion that normally functioning people are sufficiently able to be responsible despite universal causal wiring.

Harris argues that greater information makes ordinary agents resemble exculpated cases, illustrates this through an unlucky childhood, and retains responsibility only for beneficial practical effects.
Control consists in responding competently to factors one did not choose, and moral education enables people to become and maintain practically responsible self-controlling agents.
This positively defines compatibilist control and explains how causally formed people acquire autonomy, duties of self-regulation, and corresponding social freedoms.
Harris's contention that unchosen genes and environment eliminate genuine control and reduce responsibility to pragmatic behavior management.
Dennett compares agency to steering amid uncontrollable wind, argues that total causal independence is irrelevant, and links moral formation and continued self-control to practical responsibility.
A rare lapse by the most competent agent is simultaneously the strongest occasion for blame and the weakest expression of that agent's settled character, revealing luck's role.
The paradox challenges the inference from high competence to deeper authorship by arguing that anomalous failures are especially unrepresentative and adventitious.
Dennett's claim that developed competence and reliable self-control ground an adult's practical responsibility for maintaining conduct.
Harris accepts reasons-responsive differences among agents but argues that an expert's exceptionally unlikely failure says least about the expert and most clearly reflects bad luck.
Greater competence creates greater reliance-based obligations, and anomalous failure may expose correctable prior conduct rather than a paradoxical absence of responsibility.
This counters the competence paradox by grounding heightened responsibility in undertaken expectations and by treating causal diagnosis as a route to improved control.
Harris's claim that a highly competent person's rare lapse is maximally blameworthy yet minimally expressive of free agency.
Dennett argues that trusted competent agents assume special obligations, that others rely on them, and that investigating antecedents can identify failures they can subsequently correct.
Tracing an anomalous lapse to earlier conduct merely uncovers further unchosen causes, while accountability and public safety can be preserved without belief in ultimate self-authorship.
The move answers causal self-correction while presenting Harris's central proposal that social accountability need not depend on metaphysical authorship.
Dennett's argument that competent agents undertake obligations and can diagnose antecedent failures to improve their future self-control.

Harris says a radical deviation from internalized norms is unusually unrepresentative, pushes every proposed prior explanation back into causal luck, and preserves contracts and confinement pragmatically.
Limited self-authorship assembled from inherited materials is enough for moral agency, so responsible agents should accept deserved consequences despite pervasive luck.
This crystallizes the compatibilist conclusion that finite, socially embedded self-construction and accountability remain meaningful without absolute causal authorship.
Harris's position that nobody truly authors themselves and that accountability should therefore rest only on pragmatic social needs.
Dennett concedes limits and luck but maintains that people partly construct themselves, participate in shared moral practices, and cannot excuse a failure merely as cosmic misfortune.
Practical rules may treat an agent as responsible, but fuller causal knowledge would show that luck and prior causes, rather than genuine authorship, produced the particular failure.
This separates the practical usefulness of responsibility practices from the deeper claim that an individual truly authored the action, a central distinction in Harris's case.
Dennett's claim that responsible agents should accept accountability despite the pervasive role of luck in producing their conduct.

Using a missed athletic performance, Harris argues that institutions may reasonably employ responsibility heuristics even though a complete causal account would deny ultimate responsibility for the event.
Rejecting absolute responsibility does not eliminate ordinary responsibility, whose point is a pragmatic and consequentialist system of reasonable expectations, excuses, and enforceable social rules.
The passage states the core compatibilist position that responsibility worth preserving is a practical social achievement rather than metaphysical self-creation.
Harris's contention that a causally determined failure makes the actor not genuinely responsible and leaves only a pragmatic heuristic.
Dennett argues that law properly draws pragmatic lines shaped by human capacities, excusing some conditions while preserving expectations and respect for a socially valuable legal order.

If severe antisocial behavior became causally understood and reliably curable, treatment would replace retributive punishment and expose apparent evil as a condition rather than self-authored wickedness.
The cure scenario tests whether increased causal knowledge systematically erodes desert-based blame, directly supporting Harris's challenge to ultimate moral responsibility.
Dennett's pragmatic defense of responsibility practices and legal boundaries despite luck, causation, and the absence of absolute self-authorship.
Harris imagines a maximally remorseless offender transformed by a reliable intervention, arguing that successful causal treatment would make retribution seem inappropriate and medically obsolete.
Even if antisocial dispositions were diagnosable and curable, credible punishment would remain necessary because agents anticipate sanctions and shared enforcement sustains lawful cooperation.
It supplies the systemic compatibilist justification for responsibility: sanctions shape deliberation and preserve mutually understood expectations beyond rehabilitation of one offender.
Harris's claim that identifying and curing a Madoff-like causal syndrome would transform culpable wrongdoing into an exculpatory medical condition.
Dennett argues that knowledge of treatment would itself alter incentives, while dependable penalties deter wrongdoing and maintain the common expectations required by games, law, and moral life.

Deterrence may justify punishment pragmatically, yet complete causal knowledge would still dissolve personal authorship, and advance neural prediction would reveal the agent's felt control as illusory.
This passage directly joins the debate's moral-responsibility and conscious-agency strands by conceding social management while denying that it establishes genuine authorship.
Dennett's argument that dependable penalties preserve cooperation, deter dispositionally dangerous people, and thereby ground meaningful responsibility.

Harris distinguishes the practical design of justice from what agents truly are, then argues that sufficiently detailed prediction of thought and action would shatter the subjective sense of authorship.

Neuroscientific decoding does not yet provide real-time foreknowledge, and prediction that interacts with its subject faces principled self-referential limits, so current findings do not establish the proposed authorship-destroying scenario.
The argument challenges a key empirical and conceptual premise of Harris's prediction thought experiment, limiting its force against conscious agency and authorship.
Harris's claim that neuroscience could know each thought and action before the subject does and thereby expose conscious authorship as an illusion.
Dennett distinguishes retrospective data analysis from genuine live prediction and adds that an interacting predictor must include its own behavior, creating theoretical limits on complete forecasts.

If a complete record of a person's words could be produced before conscious awareness, that foreknowledge would undermine free will because consciousness enters too late to originate the unfolding action.
The thought experiment isolates Harris's central first-person objection: prior determination and preconscious neural formation conflict with the experience of consciously originating action.
Dennett's objection that present experiments lack real-time predictive power and that an interacting complete predictor encounters self-referential limits.
Harris asks the listener to imagine an advance transcript of the conversation and argues that even short-lag mind reading would show conscious awareness following rather than directing production.
Authorship does not require conscious control of every microscopic generative step; agents author actions through practiced capacities, advance planning, and temporally extended macro-level control.
This provides the central compatibilist model of conscious agency, relocating control from instantaneous awareness of neural details to reasons-responsive, trained, extended organization.
Harris's argument that preconscious generation and advance prediction show consciousness arriving too late for a person to count as the author.

Dennett argues that predictable competence is not unfree and that artists and athletes remain authors when deliberate plans recruit trained processes whose fine-grained outputs are not consciously selected.

Compatibilism preserves a third-person notion of competence but still forfeits the first-person freedom people value, because under identical conditions the agent could not genuinely have acted otherwise.
It identifies the alleged mismatch between Dennett's functional freedom and the psychologically important libertarian capacity that Harris argues ordinary people believe they possess.
Dennett's claim that macro-level planning and trained control are sufficient for conscious authorship despite unconscious generation of particular movements or ideas.

Harris says both speakers reject libertarian metaphysics but differ over the loss involved: Dennett discounts alternative possibilities, whereas Harris treats their falsity as psychologically consequential.

An agent could have done otherwise in the relevant sense when possessing a real competence for multiple responses; demanding atom-for-atom replay mistakes deterministic identity for practical causal possibility.
This directly defends the compatibilist interpretation of alternative possibilities and rejects the identical-universe test that drives Harris's incompatibilist conclusion.
Harris's assertion that both speakers ultimately agree no one could have done otherwise, with compatibilism merely minimizing the importance of that loss.
Dennett grounds alternative possibility in an agent's range of abilities and maintains that microscopic replication is irrelevant to the causal distinctions used in ordinary deliberation and action.
The ordinary felt sense of libertarian authorship presumes ultimate control, and sufficiently predictive neuroimaging would undermine that sense by revealing decisions before conscious awareness.
It supplies Harris's central experiential challenge to compatibilism: deterministic prediction would make conscious agency feel derivative even without manipulation by another person.
Dennett's earlier position that deterministic causal processes can still support meaningful alternatives and the freedom worth wanting.

Following discussion of randomness and ultimate causal ownership, Harris argues that advance prediction of deliberation would directly threaten people's experienced authorship of creative and voluntary conduct.
Deterministic chaos is not an inferior substitute for quantum indeterminacy in the free-will debate because the physical distinction between them produces no difference in moral responsibility.
The passage blocks an indeterminist escape route by arguing that replacing deterministic unpredictability with fundamental randomness cannot improve the kind of agency relevant to morality.
Harris's characterization of a coin flip as merely a surrogate for genuine randomness and his broader concern that deterministic causation defeats authentic authorship.
Dennett responds to Harris's distinction between chaotic unpredictability and true randomness by denying that the distinction changes any morally relevant feature of agency.
Because indeterminism adds nothing morally relevant, people do not need libertarian freedom; the forms of freedom genuinely worth wanting remain fully compatible with determinism.
This is the con side's motion-level conclusion, connecting the irrelevance of physical randomness to the claim that valuable human freedom survives in a deterministic world.
Harris's position that people invest heavily in libertarian authorship and that deterministic causal prediction challenges their sense of genuine agency.
After Harris clarifies that he meant only to distinguish physical kinds of randomness, Dennett argues that this distinction cannot establish a morally necessary libertarian capacity.
